title: Institutions and Citizenship
description: Ten clear, factual texts about how American public life works: a bill moving through a state legislature, checks and balances, a naturalization ceremony, a city council meeting, the census, a library board, election day at a county clerk's office, the Bill of Rights, how the FDA approves medicines, and the soldiers who once guarded Yellowstone.

lessons.title: The Long Road of a Short Bill
lessons.summary: A high school government class follows a scooter helmet bill through the state legislature, from idea to the governor's signature.
lessons.text:
Last fall, a student named Jake Ellis fell from an electric scooter near his high school. He broke his wrist, and his doctor told him he had been lucky: he had not been wearing a helmet, and his head had missed the curb by inches. When Jake came back to school, his government class decided to turn his bad luck into a lesson about how a bill becomes a law.

The kernel of their idea was simple. In their state, underage riders of bicycles had to wear helmets, but underage riders of electric scooters did not. The students wanted the same rule for both. Their teacher, Ms. Carter, explained that only a member of the legislature can introduce a bill, so the class wrote to their state senator, Linda Moreno. She liked the kernel of the idea and agreed to sponsor the bill.

Next, the bill went to a committee, a small group of senators who study bills on one subject before the whole senate votes. Ms. Carter warned the class that most bills die quietly in committee. At the hearing, Jake testified, and the questions were rigorous. One senator was openly skeptical. He asked how the police would know a rider's age, and whether parents, not the state, should decide about helmets. Jake admitted that he had no perfect answer, but he had done rigorous homework, and he showed figures from hospitals in states that already had such a law.

Then came the most dangerous moment. Another senator offered an amendment that would have required every scooter rider, of any age, to buy insurance. Ms. Carter explained that an amendment like that can torpedo a bill, because it adds costs that lead many members to vote no. Senator Moreno negotiated, and the amendment was dropped. Without it, the committee vote was unanimous: nine in favor, none against. Even the skeptical senator voted yes, saying that the students had answered his questions honestly.

After that, things went smoothly. The full senate passed the bill, and the house of representatives passed exactly the same version, so there were no differences to settle. Finally, the governor signed it, and the bill became law. Ms. Carter pointed out that the governor could have vetoed it instead, and then the legislature would have needed a two-thirds vote in each house to override the veto.

At the end of the year, Ms. Carter reminded the class that lawmakers answer to the electorate, the people who vote. "You are not part of the electorate yet," she said, "but you will be soon, and now you know how the machine works." Jake, wearing a new helmet, said that the process had not run smoothly at every step, but in the end it had worked.

Questions:
What was the kernel of the students' idea?
They wanted underage riders of electric scooters to wear helmets, just like underage riders of bicycles.
Why did the class write to Senator Moreno?
Only a member of the legislature can introduce a bill, so the class needed a senator to sponsor it.
Why can an amendment torpedo a bill?
An amendment can add costs that lead many members to vote against the bill.
What was the result of the committee vote?
The vote was unanimous: nine senators voted in favor and none voted against.
What is the electorate?
The electorate is the people who vote.

lessons.title: Three Branches and a Circle of Chairs
lessons.summary: A teacher describes the classroom game used to explain the three branches of government and checks and balances.
lessons.text:
Every September, I arrange the chairs in my classroom in a circle and divide my students into three groups. The first group plays Congress, which writes the laws. The second plays the president, who carries the laws out. The third plays the Supreme Court, which decides what the laws mean and whether they agree with the Constitution. Then I pass a question around the circle clockwise, from one branch to the next, and we watch what happens.

The question is usually small, such as a law to make the school day longer. Congress passes it. The president can sign it or veto it. After a veto, the question moves clockwise back to Congress, which can override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses. If the law survives, someone challenges it, and the question moves clockwise again, to the court, which can strike it down. By the end of the hour, the students have seen that no branch can finish the job alone.

That is the heart of checks and balances. Each branch exerts pressure on the other two, and each can rein in the others when they reach too far. The president nominates judges, but the Senate must confirm them. The courts can strike down a law, but they cannot enforce their own decisions. The branches are mutually dependent, and they keep a mutually careful eye on one another. No branch can exert its power for long without meeting the power of the other two.

Why build a government that seems designed to slow itself down? The authors of the Constitution had lived under a king, and they knew how disastrous power without limits could be. They preferred a system that was slow and noisy to one that was quick and possibly disastrous. A student once called the arrangement "a machine for making people talk to each other," and I have never found a better description.

Every year, the circle is unpredictable. Once, the "court" refused to rule at all, saying that the question was not a real legal case, which is exactly what the actual court sometimes does. Because the game is unpredictable, the students remember it, and their understanding deepens as the year goes on.

On the last day, I show the class two emblems. One is the scales of justice, the emblem of the courts: two plates in perfect balance. The other is a relay runner's baton. Every few years, one president passes the baton to the next in peace, because the law says so. That simple handing over of the baton, repeated for more than two centuries, deepens my respect for the system more than any speech could.

Questions:
How does the teacher arrange the classroom in September?
The teacher arranges the chairs in a circle and divides the students into three groups.
In which direction does the question move around the circle?
It moves clockwise, from one branch to the next.
What does it mean that each branch can rein in the others?
It means that each branch can stop the others when they try to take too much power.
Why did the authors of the Constitution want checks and balances?
They knew how disastrous power without limits could be.
What two emblems does the teacher show on the last day?
The teacher shows the scales of justice and a relay runner's baton.

lessons.title: The Morning I Became a Citizen
lessons.summary: A nurse born in Switzerland describes her naturalization ceremony and the small celebration with her family afterward.
lessons.text:
I was born in a small village in Switzerland, below an alp where my grandfather's cows spent every summer. An alp, in our part of the world, is a high mountain meadow, green in July and buried in snow by November. I moved to Ohio at twenty-six to work as a nurse. Twelve years later, after the forms, the fingerprints, the interview and the test on history and government, I received a letter with the date of my citizenship ceremony.

The ceremony took place in a federal court in Columbus. There were sixty-two of us, from thirty-one countries, sitting in rows with our families behind us. I wore a pale blue linen dress that I had bought for the day. The woman beside me, who was from Vietnam, wore a scarlet silk jacket. She told me that scarlet was a lucky color in her family.

A clerk read out the name of each country, and we stood when we heard our own. When she said "Switzerland," I was the only one who stood, and my husband and our six-year-old daughter, Mia, waved from the back. Mia waved a tiny flag over her head, several people said "aww," and Mia giggled, delighted to be noticed.

Then the judge asked us to raise our right hands, and we took the Oath of Allegiance together. I had read the words many times, but saying them out loud in a room full of strangers was different. My voice shook, and the man in front of me began to weep quietly. I had promised myself that I would not weep, but halfway through the oath I wept as well.

Afterward, the judge spoke for a few minutes. She said that we were not giving up the places we came from, but adding a new place to them. I was stunned by how much that sentence meant to me. For years I had worried that becoming a citizen here would make me less Swiss, and in one sentence she had answered the worry.

Each of us then received a certificate of citizenship, personalized with our name, photograph and date of birth. At the door, volunteers handed out personalized welcome cards written by local children. Mine said, "Welcome, Anna! Now you can vote!" Mia giggled when she saw that the child had drawn me with a crown.

We celebrated at a bakery near the court. Mia chose a cupcake with red, white and blue sprinkles, and I chose a caramel cupcake, because caramel reminds me of the candy my grandmother used to make in her kitchen below the alp. When the baker heard why we were celebrating, she said "aww" and refused to let us pay.

Questions:
What is an alp?
An alp is a high mountain meadow, green in summer and covered in snow in winter.
What did Anna wear to the ceremony?
She wore a pale blue linen dress.
Why did people in the room say "aww"?
They said "aww" because Mia waved a tiny flag over her head.
Why was Anna stunned by the judge's words?
She was stunned because for years she had worried that becoming a citizen would make her less Swiss, and the judge answered that worry.
Why did Anna choose a caramel cupcake?
Caramel reminds her of the candy her grandmother made.

lessons.title: Three Minutes at City Hall
lessons.summary: A gardener speaks during public comment at a city council meeting about a plan to spray a pesticide near a community garden.
lessons.text:
On a Saturday morning in June, Rosa Delgado was tying up tomato plants in the community garden when she reached past a rose bush and caught her thumb on a thorn. "Ow!" she said, more surprised than hurt. She was pulling out the thorn when another gardener, Tom Becker, walked over with the city newsletter.

The newsletter announced that the city council would soon vote on a plan to spray a pesticide in every city park, including the strip of park land beside the garden. The target was a moth. For two summers, the larvae of this moth had eaten the leaves of the city's oak trees, and many residents wanted the council to act.

Rosa had been a gardener for forty years, and she had spent the last ten years cultivating this garden. Thirty families shared it. Each family was free to cultivate its own small veggie plot, but the tools, the water and the bees were communal. Tom kept the bees at the edge of the garden, and every fall he turned some of their honey into mead, an ancient drink made from honey, water and yeast. Rosa worried that a pesticide strong enough to kill the moth larvae might kill the bees as well.

Rosa had never spoken at a council meeting, so she read the city's rules. The agenda was posted a week before each meeting. Any resident could sign up for public comment, and each speaker had three minutes.

On Tuesday evening, the council chamber was full. Seven council members sat at a long curved desk. When the item came up, the city's tree expert explained the plan. Then the public spoke. A father said that the moth had stripped the oak in his yard bare. Rosa spoke third. In her three minutes, she explained that the communal garden fed thirty families, that its veggie plots were full of ripe tomatoes and beans, and that the ripe fruit would be covered in spray. She asked the council to protect the trees with a method that harmed only the moth.

After public comment, one council member asked the tree expert whether such a method existed. It did: a natural spray that harms only the larvae of moths and butterflies, not bees. A member moved to use that spray and to keep a safe zone around the garden, another member seconded the motion, and it passed six to one.

Afterward, Tom shook Rosa's hand. "Three minutes," he said. "That's all democracy asked of you." The next Saturday, Rosa caught her thumb on the same rose bush and said "Ow!" again, but this time she laughed. That fall, Tom gave her a bottle of mead, and she gave him a basket of the last ripe tomatoes.

Questions:
What happened to Rosa in the garden on Saturday morning?
She caught her thumb on a thorn and said "Ow!"
Why did the city want to spray a pesticide?
The larvae of a moth had eaten the leaves of the city's oak trees for two summers.
What was communal in the garden?
The tools, the water and the bees were communal.
How long could each speaker talk during public comment?
Each speaker had three minutes.
What did the council decide?
It decided to use a natural spray that harms only the larvae of moths and butterflies, and to keep a safe zone around the garden.

lessons.title: Counting Everyone in Riverton
lessons.summary: A retired math teacher works for the census in a small river town and learns how the census counts every person.
lessons.text:
Every ten years, the Constitution requires a count of every person living in the country. The census decides how many seats each state receives in the House of Representatives, and it guides how billions of dollars in federal money are shared. Households that do not answer by mail, by phone or online receive a visit from a census worker.

In one census year, Grace Liu, a retired math teacher, took that job in Riverton, a sleepy river town where, as she liked to say, the most exciting event of the week was the arrival of the Thursday barge. In training, she learned the central rule: each person is counted where he or she lives and sleeps most of the time. A college student is counted at the dorm, not at the parents' house. A family that has lived in a motel room for months is counted at the motel, because that room is their home.

Sleepy as it was, Riverton had a little of everything: a small college with two dorms, a motel by the highway, and a dock where barges loaded with grain stopped on their way down the river. The college counted its own dorms. The motel was Grace's job. On her first afternoon, the manager introduced her to a mother and two sons who had lived in room 14 since the winter.

At the dock, she met the captain of a boat that pushed a line of six barges. His crew of mariners lived on board for four weeks at a time. Mariners on boats and ships, Grace learned, are counted in yet another special operation, so she simply reported the name of the boat.

Every answer went through validation, a set of automatic checks that look for answers that cannot be right. One week, validation found an anomaly: a small house on Elm Street seemed to hold 41 people. Grace visited and found an elderly man who lived alone. He had typed his house number, 41, into the box for the number of people. She corrected the anomaly in a minute, and they both laughed.

Grace carried a phone with the official app, but she also carried the calculator she had used in her classroom. Each evening she added up her totals on the calculator and compared them with the app. The calculator never disagreed, but she liked the habit.

Much of the count depended on outreach. Months earlier, the town's outreach committee, made up of the librarian, two pastors and the high school principal, had hung posters explaining that census answers stay confidential by law for 72 years. Grace believed that this outreach was the reason so many doors opened for her.

Questions:
Where is a college student counted in the census?
A college student is counted at the dorm, not at the parents' house.
Why was the family at the motel counted there?
They had lived in a motel room for months, so that room was their home.
How are mariners on boats counted?
They are counted in a special operation, so Grace only reported the name of the boat.
What anomaly did validation find?
It found a small house that seemed to hold 41 people, but the man had typed his house number into the wrong box.
Why did Grace think so many doors opened for her?
She believed it was because of the work of the outreach committee.

lessons.title: The Library Board Meets
lessons.summary: A new member of a public library board attends her first meeting and sees how the board decides on books, services and money.
lessons.text:
When the city council appointed Helen Brooks to the board of the public library, she imagined quiet conversations about books. Her first meeting showed her that a library board deals with almost everything.

The board had seven members, all volunteers. It approved the library's budget, set its policies and hired its director. It met in public, posted its agenda in advance and kept minutes that anyone could read.

The first item was the book budget. The director, Sandra Okafor, proposed buying more paperbacks. A paperback costs about a third as much as a hardcover, so the library could offer many more new titles. One member objected that paperbacks are less durable: their covers bend and their pages come loose after thirty or forty loans. The director answered that most popular novels are borrowed heavily for a year and then rarely, so a durable book often lasts longer than the demand for it. The board chose paperbacks for popular fiction and durable hardcovers for picture books.

The second item was a sensory room, a quiet space for children who are easily overwhelmed by noise, bright light and crowds. It would have soft lighting, walls that absorb sound, and sensory toys such as textured balls. During public comment, a mother said that her son had never managed to stay in the library longer than ten minutes. The board voted to build the room with money from a state grant.

Next came services for visually impaired residents. The library already had large-print and recorded books, but the director wanted a machine that enlarges printed pages on a screen and reads them out loud. A board member who was himself visually impaired said that it would let him read his own mail again.

There were smaller items, too. The knitting club asked to collect donated yarn in a box by the front door, and the board agreed, as long as the yarn became the hats and scarves that the club gave to a shelter. The technology manager reported that the public computers froze several times a day. Staff could reboot them, but having to reboot a computer ten times a day was no solution, so the board approved new machines.

Finally, the board discussed the annual gala, the fall dinner that raises money for the library. A local artist had donated a blue glass vase for the gala auction. One member wanted to spend the gala money on chic new furniture for the lobby. Helen, speaking for the first time, said that the old furniture was not chic, but it was comfortable, and that books mattered more. The board agreed, and the vase went on display in the lobby until the auction.

Questions:
Why did the director want to buy more paperbacks?
A paperback costs about a third as much as a hardcover, so the library could offer more new titles.
What is the sensory room for?
It is a quiet space for children who are easily overwhelmed by noise, bright light and crowds.
What machine did the director want for visually impaired residents?
She wanted a machine that enlarges printed pages and reads them out loud.
Why did the board approve new computers?
The old computers froze several times a day, and staff had to reboot them again and again.
What did the local artist donate?
The artist donated a blue glass vase for the gala auction.

lessons.title: Election Day Diary
lessons.summary: A county clerk keeps a diary of one election day, from the opening of the polls to the return of the last ballot box after midnight.
lessons.text:
4:45 in the morning. I woke before my alarm, as I do on every election day. I have been the county clerk for nine years, and in our state the clerk runs elections: my office keeps the list of registered voters, trains the poll workers, prints the ballots and counts the results. If today goes smoothly, most voters will never think about us at all, and that is the goal. Last night I pored over the list of polling places once more, although I had already pored over it a dozen times this month.

6:00. The polls opened at all 48 locations. By 6:15, the phone rang: a machine at a fire station would not start. Our technician talked the poll workers through the problem, and the machine was running ten minutes later.

7:30. Ray Dixon, our warehouse foreman, called to say that his trucks were loaded with spare machines and supplies. Ray has been our foreman for twenty-two years, and he knows every road in the county.

10:00. In the back room, ballot handlers opened mail ballots and checked each signature against the one in the voter's file. Handlers work in teams of two, and every handler signs a log each time a box of ballots moves, so that we can trace any box from the moment it arrives to the moment it is counted.

1:00 in the afternoon. A reporter asked whether we had considered letting people vote on their phones using blockchain. I told her what I had told a salesman at an election expo last spring. At the expo, his company promised that blockchain, a digital record copied across many computers, would make phone voting safe. Security experts, however, point out that blockchain cannot protect a phone that has been hacked, and phone voting leaves no paper. We prefer paper ballots, because people can count paper by hand.

7:00 in the evening. The polls closed. By law, anyone already in line at closing time may still vote, and the last voter at the library finished at 7:40.

8:30. My deputy ordered sushi for the whole staff. We ate the sushi standing up, between the machines, while results came in from the precincts.

Ten to midnight. We posted the first results, but they are not final. Over the next two weeks, an independent auditor will choose several precincts at random, and teams will count those paper ballots by hand. The auditor will then compare the hand count with the machine totals. Only after the auditor reports will a county board make the results official.

12:40. A text arrived from Ray, our foreman: "All trucks back. Every box accounted for." That is the best message a clerk can receive.

Questions:
What does the county clerk's office do in this state?
It keeps the list of registered voters, trains the poll workers, prints the ballots and counts the results.
What is Ray Dixon's job?
He is the warehouse foreman, and he has been the foreman for twenty-two years.
How do ballot handlers keep track of the ballots?
Every handler signs a log each time a box of ballots moves.
Why does the clerk prefer paper ballots to phone voting with blockchain?
Blockchain cannot protect a phone that has been hacked, and people can count paper ballots by hand.
What will the independent auditor do?
The auditor will choose several precincts at random and compare a hand count of their ballots with the machine totals.

lessons.title: Ten Short Promises
lessons.summary: An explanation of what the Bill of Rights protects, from freedom of religion and the press to fair trials and fair punishment.
lessons.text:
When the Constitution was written in 1787, many people worried that it gave the new national government great power but said little about the rights of the people. To answer that worry, Congress proposed a list of amendments, and in 1791 the states approved ten of them. Together they are known as the Bill of Rights.

The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, speech and the press, the right to gather in peace and the right to ask the government to fix a wrong. Freedom of religion works in two directions: the government may not create an official church, and it may not stop people from practicing their faith. This protection covers the smallest sect as fully as the largest church. In one small town, for example, a Buddhist community wanted to build a temple for its lama, a teacher in the Tibetan tradition. The town had to treat the temple of the lama exactly as it would treat any other house of worship. A sect with fifty members has the same rights as a church with fifty thousand.

Freedom of speech protects even ideas that most people dislike. A group may publish a manifesto that nearly everyone finds foolish, and the government may not punish its members for the manifesto itself. The founders had seen colonial officials attempt the suppression of pamphlets and newspapers, and they believed that the suppression of ideas was more dangerous than the ideas themselves. Speech that threatens violence, however, is not protected.

Freedom of the press protects investigative reporters, who spend months studying public records and talking to witnesses in order to uncover problems that officials would prefer to hide. When an investigative story uncovers deception in a city contract, such as a company billing the city for work it never did, the press is doing exactly what the founders hoped. Exposing deception is one of its oldest jobs.

The Fourth Amendment protects people against unreasonable searches. The police usually need a warrant from a judge to search a home, even when they are looking for a fugitive. A fugitive may be dangerous, and in a true emergency officers may act quickly, but as a rule a judge, not an officer alone, decides.

The Fifth and Sixth Amendments protect people accused of crimes: they have the right to remain silent, the right to a lawyer and the right to a quick, public trial before a jury. The Eighth Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishment. Behind it lies an old idea: punishment by the state should be justice, not vengeance. A crowd may want vengeance, but the law asks for fairness, even toward people who have done terrible things.

The last two amendments add that people keep rights the list does not name, and that powers not given to the national government belong to the states or to the people.

Questions:
Why was the Bill of Rights written?
Many people worried that the Constitution said little about the rights of the people.
Does the First Amendment protect only large churches?
No, it protects the smallest sect as fully as the largest church.
What do investigative reporters do?
They study public records and talk to witnesses to uncover problems that officials would prefer to hide.
Do the police need a warrant to search a home for a fugitive?
Usually yes, although in a true emergency officers may act quickly.
What old idea lies behind the Eighth Amendment?
Punishment by the state should be justice, not vengeance.

lessons.title: How a Medicine Reaches the Pharmacy
lessons.summary: A pharmacist explains to a high school class how the FDA approves new medicines and how it treats supplements and food labels.
lessons.text:
Every spring, Dana Fischer, a pharmacist, visits a high school health class to answer one question: how does a new medicine get onto the shelf behind her counter? Her answer begins with a federal agency, the Food and Drug Administration, usually called the FDA.

Before a company may sell a new drug, it must convince the FDA of two things: safety and efficacy. Safety means that the benefits of the drug are greater than its risks. Efficacy means that the drug actually works for the condition it is meant to treat. "A drug can be perfectly safe and still have no efficacy," Dana tells the students. "Sugar pills are very safe."

Proving efficacy takes years. After laboratory tests, the company gives the drug to a small group of healthy volunteers, mainly to check its safety. Next it tests the drug on a few hundred patients to find the right dose. Finally it runs large trials with thousands of patients, some of whom receive the drug and some a pill with no medicine in it. Neither the patients nor their doctors know who received which, so the results show honestly whether the drug works.

Dana uses examples from her own shelves. One medicine treats an overly active bladder. The bladder is the organ that stores urine, and when it is overly active, it signals that it needs to be emptied far too often. In the trials, researchers counted how many fewer trips to the bathroom patients made each day. Another drug helps people who are obese to lose weight. Because people who are obese often face risks to the heart, the FDA asked the company to study patients' hearts for several years, not just their weight.

Vaccines go through the same careful review. When a company wants to offer a booster, an extra dose given months or years after the first shots, it must show that the booster restores protection that has faded.

Then she holds up a bottle of zinc tablets. Dietary supplements, she explains, do not need FDA approval before they are sold. The maker of the zinc tablets is responsible for their safety, and it may not claim that zinc cures a disease. Another bottle promises to support the thyroid gland, a small gland in the neck that helps control how the body uses energy. Its label carries a printed warning that the FDA has not evaluated its claims.

Last, she mentions food. The FDA also oversees food labels, and the law names nine foods that commonly cause allergies, including milk, eggs, peanuts and soy, which must be clearly listed. A student with an allergy to soy says that she checks every label, and Dana tells her that the law is on her side.

Questions:
What two things must a company prove before it may sell a new drug?
It must prove that the drug is safe and that it has efficacy.
What does efficacy mean?
Efficacy means that the drug actually works for the condition it is meant to treat.
What is a booster?
A booster is an extra dose of a vaccine given months or years after the first shots.
Do zinc tablets need FDA approval before they are sold?
No, dietary supplements such as zinc tablets do not need approval before they are sold.
Why does the student with an allergy check every label?
She has an allergy to soy, and soy must be clearly listed on food labels.

lessons.title: Soldiers in Yellowstone
lessons.summary: How Congress created the first national park, and how cavalry soldiers protected it for more than thirty years.
lessons.text:
In 1872, Congress did something no nation had done before: it set aside a huge area of wild land for the enjoyment of the public, forever. President Ulysses Grant signed the law, and Yellowstone became the first national park in the world. The law, however, turned out to be much easier to pass than to enforce.

Yellowstone lies mostly in Wyoming, on a high volcanic plateau. Far beneath the plateau lies an enormous mass of hot, partly melted rock. The last great eruption there happened more than 600,000 years ago, and it was so violent that it left a vast hollow in the ground. Smaller eruptions of lava followed for a long time afterward. Today the heat shows itself in geysers, which erupt when water underground boils and forces its way to the surface. The most famous geyser, Old Faithful, erupts roughly every hour and a half.

Early visitors came for this scenery: the geysers, the colorful hot springs, and a deep canyon where the Yellowstone River cascades over two great waterfalls. The taller one sends a white cascade of water more than 300 feet down into the canyon. Yet the young park had almost no money and almost no staff. Hunters shot elk and bison for their skins, and visitors broke off pieces of the geysers to take home. In 1886, Congress stopped paying for the park's civilian managers, and the Army was sent in to protect it.

The first soldiers were cavalry troopers, soldiers who rode horses. At first they lived in tents and wooden huts, and later in stone barracks at a post called Fort Yellowstone, near Mammoth Hot Springs. The troopers rode long patrols in all weather, on horses in summer and on skis in winter. In 1894, a trooper and a scout caught a man who had been killing the park's bison, which had become very rare. Within two months, Congress passed a law with real penalties for harming the park's animals.

The troopers also learned to read the land. A newborn elk calf, with pale spots on its coat, lies perfectly still in the grass, and its camouflage is so good that a rider can pass within a few feet without seeing it.

Bandits added to the troopers' work. Tourists traveled through the park in coaches pulled by horses, and in 1908 and again in 1914, a lone bandit, a different man each time, stopped a long line of coaches and robbed the passengers. The second bandit was later caught and sent to prison.

In 1916, Congress created the National Park Service, and in 1918 the last troopers rode away. The stone barracks still stand at Mammoth Hot Springs, where today they hold park offices, and visitors who come for the scenery often walk past them without knowing their story.

Questions:
What did Congress do in 1872?
It set aside a huge area of wild land as Yellowstone, the first national park in the world.
Why do geysers erupt?
They erupt when water underground boils and forces its way to the surface.
Why was the Army sent to Yellowstone?
The park had almost no money or staff, hunters were killing animals, and Congress stopped paying for its civilian managers.
Where did the troopers live?
At first they lived in tents and wooden huts, and later in stone barracks at Fort Yellowstone.
Why is it hard to see a newborn elk calf?
Its spotted coat is good camouflage, and it lies perfectly still in the grass.
